description: We are a passionate team of Artificial Intelligence students from Hyderabad, Sindh, Pakistan, interested in AI, Machine Learning, Data Science, and innovation. For NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, we are working on The Earth Information Jukebox, using technology to make NASA's Earth science data more accessible and engaging. We welcome motivated teammates skilled in Python, AI/ML, web development, data visualization, and creative problem-solving.
summary:
Listen to Earth is a web-based "Earth Jukebox" that turns NASA Earth Information
Center visualizations into sound, so you can hear our changing planet, not just
see it. Pick a visualization — such as NASA's DYAMOND Global Carbon Dioxide — and
the app reads each animation frame, measures a few visual features (dominant
colour, brightness, how much high-value data is on screen, where the activity
sits, and how much changes between frames), and drives an evolving soundscape in
real time: colour becomes melody on a pentatonic scale, brightness sets octave
and volume, intensity adds rhythmic layers, position pans the sound, and sudden
changes trigger accents.

It addresses the challenge directly by pairing every EIC visual frame with a
dynamically generated sonification, and by making the sound the primary way to
experience the data. That matters because Earth science is overwhelmingly
presented visually, which excludes blind and low-vision audiences. Here the
sonification is the accessibility feature, not an add-on: a blind user can
experience the same climate trend a sighted user sees. Full keyboard control,
screen-reader labels, and live descriptive captions make the whole jukebox
usable without sight.
details:
What it does / how it works

Listen to Earth converts NASA Earth Information Center visualizations into a real-time soundscape. A Python data pipeline downloads NASA's DYAMOND Global CO2 visualization (SVS #5196), extracts animation frames using FFmpeg, and calculates five features per frame: dominant hue, brightness, high-value data coverage, horizontal activity position, and frame-to-frame change.

These features control the sound. Hue selects musical notes from a C-major pentatonic scale, brightness controls octave and volume, data intensity creates rhythmic layers, horizontal position controls stereo panning, and significant changes trigger chime accents.

The application also sonifies real GMAO DYAMOND Phase II NetCDF CO2 data. Users can experience the generated sound through the browser or offline WAV audio.

Benefits and impact

Earth science is usually presented visually, which creates accessibility barriers for blind and low-vision audiences. Listen to Earth makes sound the primary way to experience NASA Earth data. It provides keyboard controls, screen-reader-friendly captions, and high-contrast features, making scientific information more accessible.

Tools and technologies

  • Backend: Python, FastAPI
  • Data processing: NumPy, Pillow, xarray, NetCDF4
  • Video processing: FFmpeg
  • Frontend: React, Vite, JavaScript
  • Audio: Tone.js, Web Audio API
  • Visualization: HTML5 Canvas
  • Deployment: Github Pages

Creativity and innovation

Our project creatively translates visual patterns and scientific data into sound. Each sound parameter represents a specific data feature, making the sonification understandable and meaningful. We use a pentatonic scale to maintain musical harmony while preserving changes in the data. Precomputed features help the application run efficiently, including on lower-end devices.
